title: Primeros pasos: Sounds, Greetings & Courtesy
summary: Learn Spanish pronunciation, respectful greetings, and the core words needed to register a patient.

lessons.title: Spanish Pronunciation and the Alphabet for Spelling Names

levels.kid:
Spanish is a friendly language to read out loud. Most letters make the same sound every time. The five vowels are like five little bells: **a** (ah), **e** (eh), **i** (ee), **o** (oh), **u** (oo). They never change their song.

Some letters are tricky. The **h** is silent, like a ninja. So "hola" sounds like "OH-lah." The **ñ** has a little wave on top and sounds like "ny," as in "niño" (NEE-nyoh), which means child.

Doctors who speak Spanish ask patients to spell their names letter by letter. Knowing the letter names, like "be" for B and "jota" for J, helps the doctor write the name just right. A correct name keeps the patient safe!
levels.hs:
Spanish spelling is very **phonetic**: words are mostly pronounced the way they are written. That makes it easier to learn than English.

**Vowels** are short and pure: a (ah), e (eh), i (ee), o (oh), u (oo). Unlike English, they do not glide into other sounds.

Key consonants:
- **h** is silent: hospital = os-pee-TAHL.
- **j** sounds like a raspy English h: jarabe (syrup) = ha-RAH-beh.
- **ll** sounds like the y in "yes" in most regions: llamar (to call).
- **ñ** sounds like "ny": año (year).
- **rr** is a rolled, trilled r: perro (dog). A single r between vowels is a quick tap: pero (but).
- **c** before e or i, and **z**, sound like s in Latin America (like "th" in much of Spain).

**Stress rules**: words ending in a vowel, n, or s stress the second-to-last syllable (en-FER-ma). Others stress the last syllable (doc-TOR). A written accent mark (tilde) breaks the rule: médico = MEH-dee-koh.

The modern Spanish alphabet has **27 letters**, including ñ. In a clinic you might ask, "¿Cómo se escribe su apellido?" (How do you spell your last name?). The patient might answer, "Ge, a, ere, ce, i, a" for García. Getting names exactly right prevents mix-ups between patients' records.
levels.college:
Accurate pronunciation and spelling are patient-safety skills: a misheard surname can split a patient's chart or attach results to the wrong person.

**The alphabet.** Since the Real Academia Española (RAE) 2010 *Ortografía*, the alphabet has 27 letters. **Ch** and **ll** are digraphs, no longer separate letters, though older patients may still recite them. Letter names for spelling:
- a, **be**, **ce**, **de**, e, **efe**, **ge**, **hache**, i, **jota**, **ka**, **ele**, **eme**, **ene**, **eñe**, o, **pe**, **cu**, **ere**, **ese**, **te**, u, **uve**, **uve doble**, **equis**, **ye**, **zeta**
- RAE recommends "ye" for y (older: "i griega") and "uve" for v. Many Latin Americans say "be larga/be grande" for B and "ve corta/be chica" for V, because **b and v sound identical**.

**Confusable pairs when spelling aloud:**
- b/v: ask "¿be de burro o ve de vaca?"
- s/c/z: identical in seseo dialects (most of Latin America).
- ll/y: merged in most speakers (yeísmo).
- silent h: "Hernández" vs "Ernández" sound the same.
- g/j before e, i: "Jiménez" vs "Giménez" are both real surnames.

**Useful phrases:**
- ¿Cómo se escribe? = How is it spelled?
- ¿Me lo deletrea, por favor? = Could you spell it for me, please?
- ¿Con tilde? = With an accent mark?
- ¿Lleva hache? = Does it have an h?

**Accent marks matter.** Written stress distinguishes words (papa = potato, papá = dad) and is part of a correct name (Martín vs Martin). Registration systems that strip tildes can still match records only if staff are consistent. Confirm double letters too: "doble ele" or "erre doble" (rr).
levels.phd:
Spanish has a near-transparent **grapheme-phoneme correspondence**, with five cardinal vowels /a e i o u/, contrasting with English's roughly 14-15 vowel phonemes. The classic learner error is English vowel reduction to schwa and diphthongization ("no" as [noʊ]); Spanish vowels stay full and monophthongal even when unstressed.

**Consonant allophony** learners rarely notice:
- /b d g/ are stops [b d g] after a pause or nasal, but **approximants** [β ð ɣ] between vowels: "dedo" (finger) is [ˈdeðo].
- /p t k/ are **unaspirated**; English aspiration is a strong accent marker.
- /t d/ are **dental**, not alveolar.
- Tap /ɾ/ vs trill /r/ contrast phonemically: pero/perro, caro/carro.
- /x/ (j, g+e/i) ranges from velar [x] to glottal [h] across Caribbean and Central American varieties.

**Dialectal mergers** directly affect dictation of names. **Seseo** (merger of /θ/ into /s/) characterizes Latin America, the Canaries and much of Andalusia; northern-central Spain keeps distinción (casa vs caza). **Yeísmo** merges /ʎ/ (ll) and /ʝ/ (y) for most speakers; Rioplatense varieties realize it as [ʃ] or [ʒ] ("calle" ~ [ˈkaʃe]). Caribbean **s-aspiration or elision** ("los ojos" > [loh ˈoho]) can obscure plural markers and final letters of names.

**Orthographic stress** follows the llana/aguda/esdrújula system: palabras **agudas** (final stress) take a tilde when ending in vowel, n, s (corazón); **llanas** (penultimate) take it otherwise (lápiz, Pérez); **esdrújulas** (antepenultimate) always do (médico). The diacritic **diéresis** (ü) marks pronounced u in güe/güi (pingüino, Agüero).

The RAE/ASALE 2010 reform fixed 27 letters and unified letter names; regional names persist, and "ch"/"ll" survive in older dictionaries and memories. Spelling dialogue therefore relies on disambiguators ("be de Barcelona"), analogous to the NATO alphabet but without a single universal standard.
levels.expert:
In clinical identity verification, Spanish names create predictable registration hazards beyond phonetics.

**Two surnames.** Most Hispanic patients carry **apellido paterno + apellido materno** (María López Ruiz). Systems with one last-name field may file her as "Ruiz," "López-Ruiz" or "López," generating duplicate medical record numbers. Ask: "¿Cuáles son sus dos apellidos?" and record both as the patient uses them. Particles (de, del, de la) and compound given names (María José, José María) are frequent sources of mis-sorting.

**Dictation strategy.** Ask the patient to spell rather than guessing from sound, and read it back: "Le repito: jota, i, eme, e, ene, e, zeta. ¿Correcto?" Use regional disambiguators the patient understands; offer "be de burro / ve de vaca." Watch for patients spelling in their own conventions: "i griega" for y, "doble ve" or "doble u" for w, "cu" for q.

**Diacritics and character sets.** Ñ and tildes are sometimes stripped by legacy electronic records (Núñez to Nunez, or corrupted encoding). Pick one institutional convention and apply it consistently; mismatched variants defeat probabilistic matching algorithms. Ñ to N changes meaning (año vs ano), so preserve it where systems allow.

**Pronouncing the name back** is also rapport: saying "Señora Ibáñez" with correct stress (ee-BAH-nyes) signals respect and reduces the risk of a patient not responding when called.

**Speech recognition and literacy.** Dictation software trained on English mangles Spanish names; review transcriptions. Some patients have limited literacy or speak an Indigenous language (Mam, K'iche', Mixteco) as their first language, with Spanish second; their names may contain sequences such as tz, x (/ʃ/) or glottal marks. Ask to see an ID document when spelling is uncertain, and use a qualified interpreter rather than improvising.

**Open issue:** no universal standard exists for transliterating these names across record systems, so cross-institution matching remains error-prone.

keyPoints: Spanish has five pure vowels: a, e, i, o, u
H is silent; J sounds like a raspy h; Ñ sounds like 'ny'
The RAE alphabet has 27 letters, including ñ
Stress rules plus the tilde tell you which syllable is loud
B/V, S/C/Z, LL/Y and silent H are confusable when spelling
Ask '¿Cómo se escribe?' and read names back to protect patient safety

advancedTest.q: A Caribbean patient says her surname sounds like [ˈbaʝeh]. What is the best registration approach?

Ask her to spell it and then read the letters back

advancedTest.q: Why might "María López Ruiz" end up with two medical record numbers?

Diacritics make her name too long for most systems
Her two surnames may be filed differently at each visit

advancedTest.q: An English speaker says "dedo" with a hard [d] twice and an aspirated [t] in "tos." What do these errors share?
choices: Both come from misreading the written tilde rules
Both result from merging the tap and trill sounds
Both show seseo applied to Spanish stop sounds
Both transfer English stop features onto Spanish
advancedTest.explain: Spanish uses an intervocalic approximant [ð] and unaspirated [t]; hard stops and aspiration are English transfers.

advancedTest.q: A system converts Núñez to Nunez. What is the most important risk?

The name gains an extra syllable when read aloud
The patient's stress shifts to the final syllable
advancedTest.explain: Mismatched spellings across visits undermine matching; a consistent institutional convention reduces duplicate records.

lessons.title: Greetings, Introductions and Usted vs. Tú

levels.kid:
When you meet someone in Spanish, you say hello first. **Hola** means "hi." In the morning you can say **buenos días**, which means "good morning."

Next, you tell them your name: **Me llamo Odin**, which means "My name is Odin."

Spanish has two ways to say "you." **Tú** is the friendly "you" for friends, family and kids. **Usted** is the polite "you" for grown-ups you don't know well, like a patient or a teacher. It's a bit like the difference between saying "hey" to your buddy and "good morning, sir" to your principal.

Doctors usually use **usted** with adult patients. It shows respect, and respect helps people trust you.
levels.hs:
Every clinical visit starts with a greeting, and in Spanish the greeting depends on the time of day:
- **Buenos días**: good morning (until about noon)
- **Buenas tardes**: good afternoon (until dark)
- **Buenas noches**: good evening or good night

To introduce yourself, say **Me llamo...** ("My name is...") or **Soy...** ("I am..."). In a clinic, add your role: **Soy estudiante de medicina** ("I'm a medical student"). To ask a patient's name, say **¿Cómo se llama usted?** When they answer, reply **Mucho gusto** ("Nice to meet you").

Spanish has two words for "you" in the singular:
- **Tú**: informal, used with friends, family, children and peers
- **Usted** (often written **Ud.**): formal, used with strangers, elders and people in authority

The choice changes the verb. "How are you?" is **¿Cómo estás?** with tú, but **¿Cómo está usted?** with usted. Usted takes the same verb form as "he/she."

Here is a real example. A doctor walks in and says: "Buenas tardes, señora. Soy la doctora Ruiz. ¿Cómo está usted?" That opening is polite, clear and respectful. The default rule for clinicians is to use **usted** with adult patients unless the patient invites you to use tú.
levels.college:
Greetings and forms of address set the tone of the clinical relationship. In many Latino cultures, **respeto** (respect) and **personalismo** (warm, personal connection) shape how trust is built, so a careful opening matters.

**Core greetings and courtesy phrases**
- **Buenos días / buenas tardes / buenas noches**: good morning / afternoon / evening
- **Mucho gusto** or **encantado/encantada**: nice to meet you (encantado agrees with the speaker's gender)
- **Por favor**, **gracias**, **de nada**: please, thank you, you're welcome
- **Con permiso**: excuse me, said before entering a room or touching someone
- **Perdón / disculpe**: sorry / excuse me, used to get attention or apologize

**Introductions**
- **Soy el doctor / la doctora...**: the definite article is used when talking *about* someone with a title, but it is dropped in direct address: "Buenos días, doctora."
- **Le presento a mi colega**: let me introduce my colleague (formal)
- **¿Cómo se llama usted?** and **¿Cómo prefiere que le llame?**: what's your name, and what would you like me to call you?

**Usted vs. tú: grammar**
- Usted is grammatically third person, so it takes the él/ella verb form: **usted tiene**, compare **tú tienes**.
- Its pronouns follow the same pattern: **le/lo/la** (third person) instead of **te**, and the possessive **su** instead of **tu**. Compare "¿Cuál es **su** nombre?" (formal) with "¿Cuál es **tu** nombre?" (informal).
- Plural **ustedes** is used for any group in Latin America. Spain also uses **vosotros** as the informal plural.

**Titles**: **señor** (Mr./sir), **señora** (Mrs./ma'am), **señorita** (Miss, usually for young unmarried women; use it with care). **Don** and **doña** go before a first name ("doña María") and show warm respect toward older adults.

Clinical default: use usted with adults. Use tú with young children and, often, with teenagers.
levels.phd:
Spanish second-person address is a classic case of the **T/V distinction** described by Brown and Gilman (1960). In their framework, pronoun choice encodes two dimensions: **power**, which is asymmetric (a superior uses T and receives V), and **solidarity**, which is reciprocal (intimates exchange T). In the twentieth century, Western European languages shifted from power toward solidarity, and reciprocal tú has spread in many settings, especially in Spain.

The historical origin of usted is **vuestra merced** ("your grace"). It contracted over time through forms such as *vuesarced* to *usted*. This is why usted takes third-person agreement: grammatically, it refers to a noun phrase, "your grace," not to "you." The same logic explains clitic pairs: **se lo explico a usted**, and the formal command **siéntese** compared with tú **siéntate**.

Regional variation is substantial:
- **Voseo**: **vos** replaces tú in Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay and much of Central America, with its own verb forms: *vos tenés*, *vos sos*.
- **Ustedeo**: in parts of Colombia (for example Boyacá and Antioquia), Costa Rica and Honduras, usted can be used even between intimates and toward children, so it marks familiarity, not distance.
- Plural: **vosotros** survives mainly in peninsular Spain. Elsewhere, **ustedes** covers both formal and informal plural address.

The forms also carry pragmatic weight. Using tú unasked with an older patient can be heard as condescending, much like **elderspeak** in English. Overly formal usted with a teenager may create distance. **Address-form accommodation**, meaning you mirror the form the patient uses, is a known sociolinguistic strategy, but asymmetry (the clinician uses usted, the patient uses tú) is common and usually acceptable.

Greetings are also politeness rituals in Brown and Levinson's sense. **Con permiso** before an examination is a **negative-politeness** move: it acknowledges the patient's autonomy and bodily space. **¿Cómo amaneció?** ("How did you wake up?") is a warm **positive-politeness** opener, common in Mexico and Central America.
levels.expert:
In practice, the opening thirty seconds of a Spanish-language encounter can raise or lower trust in ways that persist through the history and consent discussion. A reliable clinical script is:

"Buenos días, señor Pérez. Con permiso. Soy Odin, estudiante de medicina del equipo de neurocirugía. ¿Cómo prefiere que le llame?"

The script greets the patient, asks permission to enter, gives a name and role, and invites the patient to choose how they want to be addressed.

**Grammar pitfalls that learners carry into the bedside**
- **Mixing forms**: "¿Cómo está usted? ¿Tienes dolor?" This is the most common error. Once you choose usted, every verb, clitic and possessive has to agree: *¿Tiene dolor? ¿Le duele? Su mano.*
- **Article errors**: "Hola, la doctora" is wrong. Drop the article in direct address: "Hola, doctora."
- **Gender agreement**: a female speaker says *encantada*.
- **False friends**: *Estoy embarazada* means "I'm pregnant," not "I'm embarrassed." To say "I'm sorry" for a mistake, use *disculpe* or *perdone*.

**Pediatrics and families**: use tú with the child ("Hola, ¿cómo te llamas?"), usted with the parents, and *ustedes* for the whole family. Shifting between forms mid-room is normal and signals skill.

**Regional calibration**: an Argentine or Uruguayan patient who uses *vos* is not being rude. You can keep usted, and it will be understood. With a Colombian patient who uses usted with their own children, usted is not coldness. With Mexican and Central American older adults, *don/doña* plus a first name is often appreciated, but ask first.

**Honorifics and gender identity**: "¿Cómo prefiere que le llame?" avoids assuming a title. *Señorita* applied to an older woman can feel either flattering or patronizing, so *señora* is the safer default.

**Limits of a greeting**: polished courtesy phrases can make a patient overestimate your fluency, and they may then speak quickly. Saying "Hablo un poco de español; si no entiendo, le pido que repita" ("I speak a little Spanish; if I don't understand, I'll ask you to repeat") sets honest expectations. When stakes rise beyond the greeting, a qualified interpreter should be called.

keyPoints: Greet by time of day: buenos días, buenas tardes, buenas noches
Introduce yourself with Me llamo... or Soy..., plus your role
Tú is informal; usted is formal and respectful
Usted takes third-person verbs and su/le, not tu/te
Default to usted with adult patients; tú with young children
Con permiso before entering or examining shows respect

choices: It was borrowed from Latin second-person forms
It comes from 'vuestra merced,' a noun phrase
It marks solidarity rather than social power
It began as a plural of vos used for groups
advancedTest.explain: Usted derives from vuestra merced ('your grace'), which is a noun phrase, so it agrees like he or she.

advancedTest.q: A Colombian mother addresses her toddler as usted. The best interpretation is:
choices: A grammar slip that she will likely correct

advancedTest.explain: Non-reciprocal address is asymmetric. In clinics it is common and usually acceptable.

lessons.title: Numbers, Dates and Times for the Clinic

levels.kid:
Doctors use numbers all day. They need your age, your birthday and the time of your visit. In Spanish, you count like this: **uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco** (1, 2, 3, 4, 5).

To tell your age, Spanish speakers say "I **have** years." So "I am ten" becomes **Tengo diez años**: "I have ten years." Be careful with that squiggly ñ in años! It matters.

To ask the time, you say **¿Qué hora es?** The answer might be **Son las tres**: "It is three o'clock."

Here is a fun surprise. In Spanish-speaking countries, dates put the **day first**, then the month. So 2/3 means the 2nd of March, not February 3rd!
levels.hs:
Numbers come up constantly in a clinic: age, birth date, appointment times, phone numbers and the 0 to 10 pain scale (**del cero al diez**).

**Counting basics**
- 1 to 15: uno, dos, tres, cuatro, cinco, seis, siete, ocho, nueve, diez, once, doce, trece, catorce, quince.
- 16 to 29 are written as one word: **dieciséis, diecisiete, veinte, veintiuno, veintidós**.
- From 31 on, numbers use **y**: treinta y uno, cuarenta y cinco.
- 100 alone is **cien**; 120 is **ciento veinte**. 1,000 is **mil**.

**Age** uses the verb **tener** (to have): *Tengo cuarenta años* ("I am forty"). Always write **años** with ñ. Without it, *anos* means "anuses," a classic embarrassing mistake.

**Dates** go day, then month, then year: *el cinco de mayo de dos mil diez*. Months and days of the week are written in **lowercase**: lunes, martes, enero, febrero. On forms, 04/07 means **4 July**, not April 7.

**Time**: *¿Qué hora es?* For one o'clock, say **Es la una**; for other hours, **Son las dos, son las tres**. Add **y cuarto** (quarter past), **y media** (half past) or **menos cuarto** (quarter to).

Example at the front desk: *Su cita es el martes, a las diez y media de la mañana.* "Your appointment is Tuesday at 10:30 in the morning."
levels.college:
Clinical Spanish relies on numbers being precise, so learn the patterns and the traps.

**Number structure**
- 16 to 29 fuse into one word, and some carry accents: **dieciséis, veintidós, veintitrés, veintiséis**.
- 31 to 99 use three words: *setenta y ocho*.
- **Cien** stands alone or before nouns and *mil* (*cien mil*); **ciento** combines with smaller numbers (*ciento cinco*).
- Hundreds from 200 agree in gender: *doscientos hombres, doscientas mujeres*. Note the irregular forms **quinientos** (500), **setecientos** (700) and **novecientos** (900).
- **Uno** shortens to **un** before masculine nouns: *veintiún años*, *un año*.

**Age**: *¿Cuántos años tiene?* → *Tengo sesenta y dos años.* Spanish uses tener, not ser.

**Dates**
- Format: *el + day + de + month + de + year*. *Nació el doce de octubre de mil novecientos ochenta y cinco.*
- The first of the month: **el primero** (common in Latin America) or **el uno** (common in Spain).
- Written forms use **DD/MM/AAAA** (*día, mes, año*). The key term on forms is **fecha de nacimiento** (date of birth).
- Relative time: *hoy, ayer, mañana, anteayer, pasado mañana, la semana pasada*. **Hace + time** means "ago": *hace tres días*.

**Times**
- *Es la una* (singular) versus *son las cinco* (plural, because it means "the hours").
- *Y cuarto, y media, menos cuarto, menos diez*; **en punto** means sharp.
- Parts of the day: **de la mañana** (morning), **de la tarde** (afternoon to early evening), **de la noche** (night), **de la madrugada** (small hours, roughly 1 to 5 a.m.). Also *mediodía* (noon) and *medianoche* (midnight).
- Asking *when*: *¿A qué hora empezó?* → *A las ocho de la noche.*

Hospitals and official documents often use the **24-hour clock**: *las quince horas* = 3 p.m.
levels.phd:
Underneath clinical numeracy lie several structural features of Spanish that explain where learners and patients go wrong.

**Morphology and agreement.** Spanish cardinals are mostly invariable, but three behave like adjectives: *uno* (→ *un/una*), the hundreds 200 to 900 (*trescientas citas*), and compounds that end in *uno* (*veintiuna semanas*, *treinta y una semanas*). Before a feminine noun beginning with stressed *a-*, forms like *veintiún* are also heard. **Mil** is invariable (*tres mil*), while **millón** is a noun and needs *de* (*un millón de células*).

**Spelling reform.** The Real Academia Española standardized the single-word spellings of 16 to 29 (*dieciséis* rather than older *diez y seis*). Accent marks fall where the stress pattern needs them: *veintidós* is a stressed final syllable ending in -s.

**Phonological confusability.** Several pairs sound alike, especially over the phone or through a mask: **seis/siete**, **trece/treinta**, **quince/cincuenta**, **sesenta/setenta**, and **doce/dos**. Seseo, used across Latin America and parts of Spain, makes *z/c* sound like *s*. That removes a cue that could help separate *diez* from other numbers in some dialects.

**Temporal expressions.**
- *Hace + duration + que + present* expresses ongoing duration: *Hace dos semanas que me duele* ("It has hurt for two weeks"). *Desde hace dos semanas* means the same.
- *Hace + duration + preterite* means "ago": *Empezó hace dos semanas.*
- Clock time uses the definite article and agreement with an understood *hora(s)*: *la una*, *las dos*. Phrases like *a eso de las tres* or *sobre las tres* mean approximately three o'clock.

**Writing conventions.** Following RAE guidance, Spanish dates are DD/MM/AAAA, and months and weekdays are lowercase. Ordinals (*primero, segundo, tercero*) are used for floors and order, not for most dates. **Decimal separators** vary by region. Spain, Argentina, Colombia and Chile use a comma (*38,5*). Mexico, Central America and much of the Caribbean use a point. Since 2010, the RAE has accepted both.
levels.expert:
In practice, numeric errors are among the most dangerous communication failures in language-discordant care. Your goal is to make mistakes impossible, not merely unlikely.

**Safety habits**
- **Close the loop.** After a patient gives a number, repeat it back in Spanish and ask for confirmation: *¿Setenta, siete-cero?* Saying the digits separately removes the *sesenta/setenta* ambiguity.
- **Cross-check age with birth year.** Ask *¿En qué año nació?* and compare. Mismatches catch both mishearing and the registration error of transposing DD/MM.
- **Write it down.** Show the patient the time or date on paper. Many patients read numerals more reliably than they parse spoken compounds, especially those with limited formal schooling.
- **Spell out the parts of the day.** *Las siete* alone is ambiguous. Say *las siete de la mañana* or *las siete de la noche*. Some patients mean *de la tarde* well past dark, so confirm.

**Culturally loaded expressions**
- **Ocho días** often means one week, and **quince días** or **una quincena** means two weeks. Count the days aloud to clarify a follow-up interval.
- **Mañana** means both "tomorrow" and "morning." *Mañana por la mañana* is "tomorrow morning."
- Approximations such as *unos cincuenta*, *treinta y tantos* or *a eso de las tres* are honest answers. Record them as estimates rather than forcing false precision.
- **Phone numbers** are often read in pairs (*cincuenta y cinco, veintitrés...*). Ask for digits one at a time when transcribing: *dígito por dígito, por favor*.

**Documentation pitfalls.** Imported records may use a decimal comma, so *37,8* is a temperature, not two values. Spanish surnames and DD/MM dates can both scramble patient matching in electronic records. That is a known source of identification errors, so verify identity with two identifiers.

**Open questions.** Research on professional interpreters versus ad hoc interpreters shows fewer clinically significant errors when trained interpreters are used, and numbers are a frequent error category. Whether brief clinician Spanish training reduces such errors without an interpreter present is not well established. For anything consequential, use a qualified interpreter.

Age uses tener: Tengo cuarenta años, and años needs its ñ
Dates run day-month-year: 04/07 means 4 July
Months and weekdays are lowercase in Spanish
Es la una, but son las dos; add y cuarto, y media, menos cuarto
Confirm confusable numbers (sesenta/setenta) by digits, writing, and birth year

Colombia records the year of arrival instead
The patient gave two different birth dates

advancedTest.q: A transferred chart from Argentina records a temperature of "38,5." How should it be read?

advancedTest.q: You hear a patient's age as "sesenta," but the chart says 70. What is the best next step?

Record sixty since the patient said it
Ask the patient to repeat the age louder
Trust the chart and continue the visit

lessons.title: Essential Question Words: Qué, Dónde, Cuándo, Cuánto, Cómo

levels.kid:
Detectives ask questions to solve a mystery. Doctors do too! In Spanish, a few little words start almost every question.

- **¿Qué?** means "what?"
- **¿Dónde?** means "where?"
- **¿Cuándo?** means "when?"
- **¿Cuánto?** means "how much?"
- **¿Cómo?** means "how?"

A doctor might say **"¿Dónde le duele?"** That means "Where does it hurt?" The person points to a tummy or a knee.

Spanish questions have a fun trick. They start with an upside-down question mark: **¿** and end with a normal one: **?** And question words wear a little hat, an accent mark, like the one on the **é** in qué. With just five words, you can start finding clues!
levels.hs:
In a clinic, most of what you need to know comes from questions. Spanish builds them with a small set of **interrogatives** (question words). Each one carries a written **accent mark** (tilde) when it asks a question:

- **¿Qué?** What? *¿Qué le pasa?* What's wrong? (literally, what is happening to you?)
- **¿Dónde?** Where? *¿Dónde le duele?* Where does it hurt?
- **¿Cuándo?** When? *¿Cuándo empezó?* When did it start?
- **¿Cuánto?** How much? *¿Cuánto tiempo?* How long?
- **¿Cómo?** How? *¿Cómo se siente?* How do you feel?

Two other key ones: **¿Por qué?** (why?) and **¿Cuál?** (which?).

Written Spanish opens a question with **¿** and closes it with **?**. In speech, your voice usually rises at the end of a yes/no question, but with a question word the pitch often falls, much like in English.

The accent changes meaning. **Que** without an accent means "that" (*creo que sí*, I think so). **Qué** with it means "what." Likewise **como** means "I eat" or "like," but **cómo** means "how."

A real example: a patient arrives holding her side. You ask, *¿Dónde le duele?* She says, *Aquí* (here). Then: *¿Cuándo empezó el dolor?* (When did the pain start?) Two questions, and you are already building a history.
levels.college:
Spanish interrogatives are a closed class of words. With the formal **usted** forms you already use, they open most clinical questions.

**Core forms and agreement**
- **qué**: what. *¿Qué medicamentos toma?* What medications do you take?
- **dónde**: where. Use **adónde** for "to where" and **de dónde** for "from where" (*¿De dónde es usted?*).
- **cuándo**: when. *¿Cuándo fue la última vez?* When was the last time?
- **cuánto** agrees in gender and number with its noun: **cuánto tiempo**, **cuánta agua**, **cuántos días**, **cuántas pastillas**. Before a verb it stays **cuánto** (*¿Cuánto pesa?* How much do you weigh?).
- **cómo**: how. *¿Cómo es el dolor?* What is the pain like? Note that Spanish uses cómo here where English says "what... like."
- Also **quién/quiénes** (who), **cuál/cuáles** (which, and often "what" before *ser*: *¿Cuál es su nombre?*), and **por qué** (why). Its answer, **porque** (because), is written as one word with no accent.

**Word order.** The question word comes first, then the verb, then the subject if it is stated: *¿Dónde trabaja usted?* Spanish usually puts the subject after the verb.

**Accent marks.** Every interrogative carries a tilde, and so do **indirect questions**: *No sé dónde está* (I don't know where it is). The tilde tells apart **qué/que**, **cómo/como** and **dónde/donde**.

**Qué vs. cuál.** Before a noun, use qué (*¿Qué alergias tiene?*). Before *es/son* when asking for specific data, use cuál: *¿Cuál es su fecha de nacimiento?* Saying *¿Qué es su nombre?* is a classic learner error. It sounds like asking for a definition of the patient's name.
levels.phd:
Interrogatives work best when matched to the kind of information you need. Linguists separate **open (wh-) questions**, built on these words, from **closed (yes/no) questions**. Clinical interviewing makes the same split. Open questions bring out narrative, while closed questions test specific hypotheses. A good interview starts open and gradually narrows.

**Framing the chief complaint.**
- *¿Qué le trae por aquí hoy?* What brings you here today? This is the standard open opener.
- *¿En qué le puedo ayudar?* How can I help you? (literally, in what?)
- *¿Qué le pasó?* What happened to you? Use it for injuries and events.

**Mapping the interrogatives onto symptom attributes**
- Location: *¿Dónde le duele?* / *¿Hacia dónde se corre el dolor?* Where does the pain spread to?
- Onset and timing: *¿Cuándo empezó?*, *¿Desde cuándo?* (since when, which implies the problem is ongoing), *¿Cada cuánto?* (how often).
- Quantity and severity: *¿Cuánto le duele del 0 al 10?*, *¿Cuántas veces al día?*
- Quality: *¿Cómo es el dolor?* Offer options such as *punzante, ardoroso, opresivo* (stabbing, burning, pressing).
- Modifying factors: *¿Qué lo mejora? ¿Qué lo empeora?* What makes it better or worse?

**Grammar nuances**
- **Prepositions come first**, never at the end. *¿Con quién vive?* (Who do you live with?) cannot be built like the English sentence.
- **Desde cuándo** takes the present tense for ongoing states: *¿Desde cuándo tiene fiebre?* Using the preterite here is a common learner error.
- **Cómo** can mean "what" when you didn't hear something: *¿Cómo?* = Pardon? This is gentler than *¿Qué?*, which can sound abrupt in some regions.
- **Exclamatives** use the same accented words: *¡Qué bien!* (How good!).

**Pragmatics.** In many Latin American varieties, a bare *¿Qué?* can sound curt. Softeners make you sound more respectful: *¿Me puede decir...?* (Can you tell me...?), *Disculpe, ¿cómo dijo?* (Sorry, what did you say?).
levels.expert:
With fluent clinicians, the failures are rarely about vocabulary. They come from question design and from false friends hiding inside familiar question frames.

**High-yield pitfalls**
- **Stacked questions.** *¿Cuándo, dónde y cómo empezó?* overloads the patient and gets you a partial answer. Ask one interrogative per turn. This matters even more through an interpreter, who may not render all three.
- **Ambiguous cuánto.** *¿Cuánto toma?* can mean "how much do you drink" or "how much (medication) do you take." Name the object: *¿Cuánto alcohol toma por semana?* Asking about quantity without units invites guesses, so ask for frequency: *¿Cuántos días a la semana?*
- **Embarazada vs. avergonzada.** *¿Está embarazada?* asks "Are you pregnant?" It does not ask about embarrassment.
- **Cómo le va / cómo está** is a social greeting. It does not invite a review of symptoms. For a clinical opening, use *¿Cómo se ha sentido?* (How have you been feeling?).
- **Low-literacy pain scales.** *¿Cuánto le duele del 0 al 10?* often fails. Pair it with verbal anchors: *¿Poco, más o menos, o mucho?*

**Teach-back uses the same words.** To check understanding at the end of a visit, use open interrogatives rather than *¿Entiende?*, which almost always gets a polite *sí*:
- *¿Cómo va a tomar esta medicina?*
- *¿Cuándo debe regresar?*
- *¿Qué señales le harían volver a urgencias?* What signs would make you return to the emergency room?

**Regional variation.** *¿Qué tanto?* (Mexico, Central America) is common for "how much." *¿Qué onda?* is slang and not suitable for the clinic. In the Caribbean, the subject often comes before the verb: *¿Qué tú quieres?*

**Neuro relevance.** Orientation questions are themselves built on interrogatives: *¿Dónde estamos?*, *¿Qué día es hoy?*, *¿Cómo se llama?* Confused answers can reflect delirium or aphasia rather than a language barrier. Telling these apart requires a qualified interpreter, not a family member.

**Open question.** It remains unclear how much non-native question phrasing affects patient disclosure. Studies link language-concordant care to better outcomes, but the role of question-level fluency has not been well isolated.

Questions open with ¿ and close with ?
Question words carry an accent: qué vs. que, cómo vs. como
Cuánto agrees with its noun: cuánta, cuántos, cuántas
Use cuál, not qué, before es: ¿Cuál es su nombre?
Ask one open question at a time, then narrow

lessons.title: Patient Registration: Name, Age, Address and Contact Details

levels.kid:
When you visit a doctor, someone at the front desk writes down who you are. In Spanish, they might ask:

- **¿Cómo se llama?** (What is your name?)
- **¿Cuántos años tiene?** (How old are you?)
- **¿Dónde vive?** (Where do you live?)

You could answer: **Me llamo Ana.** (My name is Ana.) **Tengo nueve años.** (I am nine years old.)

Here is a fun surprise. In Spanish, you don't say "I am nine." You say "I **have** nine years!" Tener means "to have."

The desk also asks for a phone number, **número de teléfono**, so the clinic can call your family. Writing everything down carefully helps the doctor take care of the right person.
levels.hs:
**Registration** (*el registro*) is the first step of a clinic visit: collecting the patient's identifying details. In Spanish, polite registration uses the formal **usted** form.

Core questions:
- **¿Cuál es su nombre completo?** What is your full name?
- **¿Cuántos años tiene?** How old are you? Answer: *Tengo 45 años.* Spanish uses **tener** (to have) for age, not *ser* (to be).
- **¿Cuál es su fecha de nacimiento?** What is your date of birth?
- **¿Cuál es su dirección?** What is your address?
- **¿Cuál es su número de teléfono?** What is your phone number?

A key cultural point: many Spanish speakers have **two surnames** (*apellidos*). The first comes from the father, the second from the mother. A patient named **María Elena García López** has the paternal surname García and the maternal surname López. If staff file her under "López," her records may be split or lost. Ask: *¿Cuáles son sus apellidos?* (What are your surnames?)

Note the trap: **dirección** means "address" here, not "direction" in the sense of instructions. And *¿Cuál es...?* (not *¿Qué es...?*) is used to ask for a specific piece of information like a name or number.

Accurate registration protects patient safety, because two identifiers (usually name and date of birth) are used to confirm identity before treatment.
levels.college:
Registration in Spanish combines a small set of high-frequency structures with cultural knowledge about names and addresses.

**Name.** *¿Cómo se llama (usted)?* uses the reflexive *llamarse* ("to call oneself"); the answer is *Me llamo...* For records, ask for *nombre(s)* (given names) and *apellidos* (surnames). Hispanic naming conventions:
- **Primer apellido** (paternal) + **segundo apellido** (maternal): Juan Carlos **Pérez Ramírez**.
- Filing is by the first surname: *Pérez Ramírez, Juan Carlos*.
- Some married women add *de* + the husband's surname (*Ana Ruiz de Torres*), though this is declining.
- Compound given names (*María José*, *José María*) are a single name, not a first and middle name.

**Age and birth date.** *¿Cuántos años tiene?* uses *tener*. *¿Cuál es su fecha de nacimiento?* Dates in Spanish are spoken and often written **day/month/year**: *el 3 de mayo de 1980* = 03/05/1980. A US form expecting MM/DD can therefore scramble the date.

**Address.** *¿Cuál es su dirección?* Spanish order is street, then number: *Calle Olmo, número 25*. Useful terms: *calle* (street), *avenida* (avenue), *apartamento* (apartment), *ciudad* (city), *código postal* (ZIP code).

**Contact.** *número de teléfono / celular* (Latin America) or *móvil* (Spain); *correo electrónico* (email). Phone numbers are often read in pairs: *veinticinco, treinta y ocho...*

**Emergency contact and insurance.** *¿A quién llamamos en caso de emergencia?* (Whom do we call in an emergency?) *¿Tiene seguro médico?* (Do you have health insurance?)

Confirm with read-back: *Repito: García López, María Elena. ¿Es correcto?*
levels.phd:
Registration is a high-stakes linguistic task because identification errors propagate through the record. The Joint Commission's patient-safety goals require **two patient identifiers**, typically name and date of birth. In Spanish-speaking populations, both identifiers are vulnerable to systematic error.

**Surname mismatch.** Hispanic double surnames (*apellido paterno* + *apellido materno*) collide with Anglo systems built for one surname. Typical failures include filing under the maternal surname, hyphenating inconsistently (*García-López* vs *García López*), or dropping a surname. Each produces **duplicate records**, a recognized source of missed allergies, repeated tests and misattributed results. Spanish law has allowed parents to choose surname order since 1999, and since 2017 order is agreed rather than defaulting to paternal-first, so "first surname = father's" is a strong heuristic, not a rule.

**Date format.** Spanish uses **DD/MM/AAAA** (*año*). For days 1-12, 04/07 is ambiguous: 4 July or 7 April. The safest practice is spoken confirmation with the month name: *¿Nació el cuatro de julio?*

**Grammar for precise questioning.**
- *¿Cuál es su...?* asks for a specific item from a set (name, number). *¿Qué es...?* asks for a definition, so *¿Qué es su nombre?* is a common learner error.
- Age uses *tener*; ages over twenty use compounds like *treinta y cinco*. *Veintiuno* drops to *veintiún* before a masculine noun (*veintiún años*).
- Phone numbers are commonly grouped in pairs, which taxes number comprehension. Asking *dígito por dígito, por favor* reduces error.

**Orthography.** Spelling names aloud needs the alphabet: *be larga/be grande* (B) vs *ve corta/uve* (V), *doble ve* (W), and the distinct letter *eñe* (Ñ). Accent marks (*Martínez*, *Ramírez*) are part of the name, but many systems strip them, which can affect record matching.
levels.expert:
In practice, registration Spanish should sound respectful, scripted and verifiable. A natural sequence at the desk:

- *Buenos días. Voy a hacerle unas preguntas para su registro.* (I'll ask you some questions for your registration.)
- *¿Me puede decir su nombre completo, con los dos apellidos?* (Can you tell me your full name, with both surnames?)
- *¿Me lo deletrea, por favor?* (Would you spell it for me?) Note the clitic pair *me lo*.
- *¿Y su fecha de nacimiento: día, mes y año?* Naming the order prevents DD/MM inversion.
- *¿Cuál es su domicilio actual?* *Domicilio* is the formal/legal word for residence.
- *¿Hay un número donde podamos dejarle un mensaje?* Uses the subjunctive *podamos*, which is natural after an indefinite antecedent.

**Grammar notes.** The *usted* object pronoun *le* (*hacerle*, *dejarle*) attaches to infinitives. Softened requests with *¿Me puede...?* or the conditional *¿Podría...?* sound more courteous than bare commands.

**Pitfalls.**
- Do not require an address or ID in a way that suggests immigration screening. Phrase it neutrally, for example *Lo pedimos solo para poder contactarle* (We ask only so we can contact you). Fear of disclosure lowers care-seeking. Know your institution's policy and whether a field is truly required.
- *Sexo* vs *género*: forms increasingly separate these. Ask *¿Cómo prefiere que me dirija a usted?* (How do you prefer I address you?).
- Indigenous-language speakers (for example K'iche', Mixtec or Mam speakers from Guatemala and Mexico) may have limited Spanish. Spanish registration does not guarantee that the patient understands, and a qualified interpreter in the right language may be needed.
- Avoid false friends: *dirección* is address, but *dirección* also means management. *Estado civil* means marital status (*soltero/a, casado/a, divorciado/a, viudo/a, unión libre*).

**Open questions.** Probabilistic matching algorithms in electronic records perform worse on Hispanic names, and research on name-standardization fields (separate paternal and maternal surname boxes) is still developing. Reliable bilingual registration remains an equity issue, not only a clerical one.

keyPoints: Ask for the name with ¿Cómo se llama? or ¿Cuál es su nombre completo?
Spanish states age with tener: Tengo 45 años
Many patients have two surnames, paternal first, then maternal
Spanish dates run day/month/year, so confirm the month by name
Dirección means address; use ¿Cuál es...? to ask for specific data
Read details back to confirm two patient identifiers

test.q: Which question asks a patient's age?
test.explain: ¿Cuántos años tiene? literally asks 'How many years do you have?' The others ask for an address, a name and insurance.

test.q: Spanish expresses a person's age with which verb?
test.explain: Spanish says Tengo 45 años ('I have 45 years'). Using ser for age is a common English-speaker error.

test.q: For María Elena García López, which is the paternal surname?
test.explain: By convention the first surname (García) is paternal and the second (López) is maternal.

test.q: A patient's record should usually be filed under which name?
test.explain: Filing is by the first surname, for example Pérez Ramírez, Juan Carlos. Filing under the second surname creates duplicate records.

test.q: In a registration context, dirección means:
test.explain: ¿Cuál es su dirección? asks for an address. The word is not about giving directions or instructions here.

test.q: A Spanish speaker writes a birth date as 04/07/1990. It most likely means:
test.explain: Spanish uses day/month/year, so 04/07 is 4 July. That is why staff confirm the month by name.

test.q: Why is ¿Qué es su nombre? considered a learner error?
choices: Qué is too informal for adult patients
Su refers to a third person, not to you
Qué asks for a definition, not an item
Nombre is the wrong word for a name
test.explain: ¿Cuál es...? requests a specific piece of information. ¿Qué es...? asks what something is, as in a definition.

test.q: What does código postal mean?
test.explain: Código postal is the postal or ZIP code. Correo electrónico means email.

test.q: Why do clinics confirm two identifiers such as name and birth date?
choices: To fill a legal form for visitors
To decide which language to use
To prevent errors in identifying patients
test.explain: Two identifiers reduce mix-ups between patients, which can lead to wrong treatments or misfiled results.

test.q: What is the Spanish word for 'surnames'?
test.explain: ¿Cuáles son sus apellidos? asks for both surnames.

test.q: To answer '¿Cómo se llama?', you say: Me ___ Ana.
test.explain: Me llamo comes from the reflexive verb llamarse, 'to call oneself.'

test.q: What Spanish phrase means 'date of birth'?
test.explain: ¿Cuál es su fecha de nacimiento? asks for the date of birth.

kidTest.q: What does '¿Cómo se llama?' ask?
kidTest.explain: It asks 'What is your name?'

kidTest.q: In Spanish, how do you say you are nine years old?
kidTest.explain: Spanish says 'I have nine years,' using tener.

kidTest.q: What does 'número de teléfono' mean?
kidTest.explain: The clinic uses it to call your family.

kidTest.q: Why does the front desk write down your details?
choices: To pick a prize for you
To help the right person get care
kidTest.explain: Writing things carefully helps the doctor care for the right person.

kidTest.q: Fill in the Spanish word for 'I have': '_ _ _ _ _ nueve años.' (Hint: t _ _ _ _)
kidTest.explain: Tengo means 'I have.' Spanish uses it for age.

advancedTest.q: A clinic's system stores one surname field. Which outcome is most likely for Hispanic patients?
choices: Dates of birth recorded in day/month/year format
Duplicate records from inconsistent surname entry
Accent marks are added automatically to most names
Faster matching because fewer fields exist
advancedTest.explain: Forcing double surnames into one field leads to inconsistent entry, which splits records. Duplicate records can hide allergies and results.

advancedTest.q: Which question best prevents a day/month inversion when getting a birth date?
choices: ¿Y su fecha de nacimiento: día, mes y año?
¿Me puede escribir la fecha con números?
¿Cuál es su dirección actual, por favor?
advancedTest.explain: Naming the order (día, mes, año) and then confirming the month by name removes ambiguity. Writing digits alone keeps the DD/MM problem.

advancedTest.q: Why does 'donde podamos dejarle un mensaje' use the subjunctive?
choices: Usted forms require the subjunctive in questions
Dejar is irregular and lacks an indicative form
Any polite request needs the subjunctive mood
It follows an indefinite, possibly nonexistent antecedent
advancedTest.explain: The speaker doesn't know whether such a number exists. An indefinite antecedent triggers the subjunctive in the relative clause.

advancedTest.q: A Mam-speaking patient answers registration questions briefly in Spanish. The best inference is:
choices: Mam and Spanish are dialects of one language
Address questions should simply be skipped
A qualified interpreter in Mam may be needed
advancedTest.explain: Indigenous-language speakers may have limited Spanish, so short answers don't prove understanding. An interpreter in the patient's language supports safe care.
